By Paul Shoemaker · October 27, 2026

Reading the Swift River's older landscape

A preliminary field-analysis guide—not a list of places to dig.

Begin with the case study and research map. The following is Gold Trails' proposed observation routine, not a field-tested recovery method.

1. Establish access before choosing a sample

A road crossing, public rest stop, or map polygon does not establish rights to enter adjoining land or remove material. Confirm the landowner or manager, mineral rights where relevant, the exact permitted activity, and any current local restrictions. Keep permission and its date in your private notes. We have not verified parcel-by-parcel access for the study window.

Maine's 38 M.R.S. §480-Q(5) exempts gold panning from that permit requirement only when banks are not disturbed and no unlicensed discharge is created. This is not a blanket exemption from property, habitat, municipal, or land-manager rules. Motorized prospecting has separate conditions under subsection 5-A and is outside this preliminary guide. The Maine Geological Survey's access overview directs prospectors to landowners and the responsible agencies.

2. Describe the landform before naming it

From a safe, authorized viewpoint, look for a flat surface above the stream, a break in slope, exposed sediment layering, or a hollow disconnected from today's flow. Photograph with a scale and a direction. Record “possible terrace” rather than promoting a shape into a confirmed former riverbed.

Check the mapped unit. Qst is a survey interpretation of reworked valley deposits; Pt describes till. A deposit can include more than one sediment history. Do not cut into a bank to reveal the sequence.

3. Keep the clocks separate

Record the source map's publication date, any dated photograph, and the proposed geological period in separate fields. A 2021 map can describe a glacial feature; it does not make the feature 2021 years old. A recent cutoff seen between two photographs is different evidence from a broadly glacial meltwater channel.

A terrace's height alone does not give its age. If measuring relative elevation later, retain the modern-stream reference, vertical datum, instrument, and uncertainty. This guide supplies no measured terrace heights.

4. Test a permitted contact, not a whole story

Only where the exact location and method have been authorized, consider small, fixed-volume samples of already accessible loose material. Compare the proposed contact with nearby control gravel using the same recovery method. Label them separately; record zero results and uncertain identifications as well as visible gold.

Do not excavate terrace faces, strip roots or vegetation, undermine boulders, or enter dangerous current. If a question requires such disturbance, leave it as an unanswered research question. Restore permitted disturbances according to the applicable rules and landowner conditions.

Our existing test-pan comparison article explains why equal starting volumes and separate notes matter.

A notebook entry you can reuse

Record Include
Access Owner/manager permission, permitted method, date, restrictions
Position Private location reference; current river versus mapped feature
Deposit Unit code, observed grains, sorting, layering and contact
Time Photo/map date; geological age if established; otherwise unknown
Test Fixed sample volume, recovery method, control and repeat
Outcome Gold observed, none observed, or uncertain; losses and limitations

Keep exact sample locations private unless publication is appropriate and authorized. A useful negative result is better than a confident story unsupported by the sediment.

Checked October 27, 2026: statutory text in §480-Q(5) and the linked agency overview. This is a preliminary guide; site-specific permissions and restrictions remain to be confirmed.
